message.content: In lions, one of the most striking examples of a dominant genetic trait is the presence and size of the mane in adult males. The genes that control mane development (including those related to androgen receptors and hair follicle growth) are expressed dominantly, meaning that even a single copy of the relevant allele can produce a full‑grown mane. This is why male lions almost always have manes, whereas females do not—because the female’s genotype lacks the dominant alleles that trigger mane growth.
